steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper benchmarking BERT-based transformer models on embedded devices for NLP tasks like intent classification, sentiment classification and NER, looking at the accuracy vs. resource trade-offs. End with our contributions and key findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: NLP on embedded / offline devices
- BERT models and why deploying them on embedded systems is hard
- Developer's problem: which architecture to choose
- Our exploratory study and research questions
- Contributions
- Key findings and paper roadmap

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - NLP and large language models transforming interaction with technology
  - IoT apps -> growing demand for voice-controlled services
  - use cases: home automation, healthcare, industrial control, automotive infotainment
  - need models that (a) run on the hardware, (b) meet desired accuracy
  - digital assistants (Alexa, Siri, Cortana) use cloud; offline home/industrial robots, automotive infotainment, battlefield/military equipment may lack connectivity
  - challenge: feasibility of large language model on resource-limited devices
- BERT and embedded deployment
  - Transformer architectures, BERT-based models: SOTA baselines for IC, SC, NER
  - criticism: data-hungry, memory and energy heavy
  - BERT_{Base}: 431 MB, 110 M parameters -> often impractical, esp. production with minimum accuracy
  - lighter versions (DistilBERT, TinyBERT) lose accuracy; depends on task difficulty; emerging entity, mixed emotion detection
  - inevitable trade-off; developers lack insight, trial-and-error
- Developer's perspective
  - unclear what "right" BERT architecture is for a task
  - we try distilled models (DistilBERT, TinyBERT) for IC, SC, NER
  - ready-to-use distilled models poor on some SC and NER datasets (Sec. 4) -> explore other models
- Our study
  - exploratory study under resource constraints and accuracy budgets
  - questions: (a) suitable architecture for target hardware + user-defined requirements (accuracy, inference time); (b) accuracy vs. model size trade-off with optimizations such as pruning; (c) implications of pruning on accuracy, memory, inference time, energy
  - four hardware: Raspberry Pi, Jetson Nano, UP 2, UDOO
  - some distilled models failed performance goals (F1); pruning reduces size but not energy

  - fills gap between simulation-based studies and real-world scenarios; no prior deployment on embedded platforms
  - helps designers choose architectures; implementation and docs public
  - four platforms, 2 GB and 4 GB RAM variants; complexity vs. accuracy (Sec. 3 - Sec. 4)
  - three metrics: inference time, memory usage, energy; lookup table for designers (Sec. 4)

  - IC: 90%+ F1
  - inference time proportional to model size; trimming loses accuracy (60% size reduction -> 50% accuracy loss)
  - energy consistent with or without pruning
  - GPUs reduce inference time, faster CPUs can compensate
  - roadmap: Sec. 2 problem statement and datasets, Sec. 3 setup, Sec. 4 findings

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Natural language processing (NLP) and the emergence of large language models are quickly changing how we interact with technology. Because there are more and more IoT-specific applications, there is a growing demand for voice-controlled services that do tasks by responding to spoken commands. Use cases of NLP applications, especially ones that need embedded and mobile systems, include home automation, healthcare, industrial control, and automotive infotainment. If we want to design a dialogue-based interaction system for a target device, we need models that (a) can run on the hardware and (b) meet the desired accuracy. Some services such as digital assistants (e.g., Alexa, Siri, Cortana) can use cloud resources to process human voices, but there are applications (e.g., offline home/industrial robots, automotive infotainment, battlefield/military equipment) that may not have network connectivity, so the NLP tasks have to run on the embedded device itself. The challenge is to understand if it is feasible to run a large language model on devices with limited resources.

Transformer-based architectures, and especially BERT-based models, are popular state-of-the-art baselines for many NLP tasks, for example Intent Classification (IC), Sentiment Classification (SC), and Named Entity Recognition (NER). But a well-known criticism of BERT-based architectures is that they are data-hungry and use a lot of memory and energy, so it is challenging to deploy them in embedded systems. Because of its big size (431 MB) and number of parameters (110 M), deploying a pre-trained BERT model (BERT_{Base}) on resource-constrained embedded devices is often impractical, especially at production level where there are minimum accuracy/performance requirements. Lighter versions of BERT (e.g., DistilBERT and TinyBERT) often lose accuracy. How much the performance degrades depends on how difficult the task is, since these models often do not perform well on complex NLP tasks like emerging entity or mixed emotion detection. So designers have to make a trade-off between an accurate model and one that runs smoothly in a resource-constrained environment. Developers often do not know much about this trade-off and spend a lot of time on trial-and-error experiments to find an architecture that works on the target hardware and meets the accuracy they want.

For a developer, it is still not clear what the "right" BERT-based architecture is for a given NLP task, one that gives a good trade-off between the available resources and the minimum accuracy the user wants. Since the BERT_{Base} model is so big, we try different "distilled" BERT models (e.g., DistilBERT and TinyBERT) for IC, SC, and NER tasks. However, the existing ready-to-use distilled models do poorly on some SC and NER datasets (Sec. 4). So other models need to be explored that can optimize the efficiency/accuracy trade-offs better.

- Our study
  - exploratory study of BERT models under resource constraints / accuracy budgets
  - questions (a) right architecture for hardware + accuracy and inference time requirements, (b) accuracy vs model size with pruning, (c) pruning effects on accuracy, memory, inference time, energy
  - four boards: Raspberry Pi, Jetson Nano, UP 2, UDOO
  - distilled models missed F1 goals on some tasks; pruning does not help much with energy
- Contributions
  - no prior work deployed these models on embedded platforms; fills gap with simulation studies; code public
  - four platforms with 2 GB and 4 GB RAM (Sec. 3 - Sec. 4)
  - inference time, memory, energy; lookup table (Sec. 4)
- Key findings
  - IC 90%+ F1; 60% smaller model -> 50% less accuracy; energy about the same with pruning; faster CPUs can make up for no GPU
- Roadmap: Sec. 2, Sec. 3, Sec. 4

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Natural language processing (NLP) and the emergence of large language models are quickly changing how we interact with technology. Because there are more and more IoT-specific applications, there is a growing demand for voice-controlled services that do tasks by responding to spoken commands. Use cases of NLP applications, especially ones that need embedded and mobile systems, include home automation, healthcare, industrial control, and automotive infotainment. If we want to design a dialogue-based interaction system for a target device, we need models that (a) can run on the hardware and (b) meet the desired accuracy. Some services such as digital assistants (e.g., Alexa, Siri, Cortana) can use cloud resources to process human voices, but there are applications (e.g., offline home/industrial robots, automotive infotainment, battlefield/military equipment) that may not have network connectivity, so the NLP tasks have to run on the embedded device itself. The challenge is to understand if it is feasible to run a large language model on devices with limited resources.

Transformer-based architectures, and especially BERT-based models, are popular state-of-the-art baselines for many NLP tasks, for example Intent Classification (IC), Sentiment Classification (SC), and Named Entity Recognition (NER). But a well-known criticism of BERT-based architectures is that they are data-hungry and use a lot of memory and energy, so it is challenging to deploy them in embedded systems. Because of its big size (431 MB) and number of parameters (110 M), deploying a pre-trained BERT model (BERT_{Base}) on resource-constrained embedded devices is often impractical, especially at production level where there are minimum accuracy/performance requirements. Lighter versions of BERT (e.g., DistilBERT and TinyBERT) often lose accuracy. How much the performance degrades depends on how difficult the task is, since these models often do not perform well on complex NLP tasks like emerging entity or mixed emotion detection. So designers have to make a trade-off between an accurate model and one that runs smoothly in a resource-constrained environment. Developers often do not know much about this trade-off and spend a lot of time on trial-and-error experiments to find an architecture that works on the target hardware and meets the accuracy they want.

For a developer, it is still not clear what the "right" BERT-based architecture is for a given NLP task, one that gives a good trade-off between the available resources and the minimum accuracy the user wants. Since the BERT_{Base} model is so big, we try different "distilled" BERT models (e.g., DistilBERT and TinyBERT) for IC, SC, and NER tasks. However, the existing ready-to-use distilled models do poorly on some SC and NER datasets (Sec. 4). So other models need to be explored that can optimize the efficiency/accuracy trade-offs better.

In this research we do an exploratory study of BERT-based models under different resource constraints and accuracy budgets, to get empirical data about these resource/accuracy trade-offs. We want to answer these questions: (a) how can we find the suitable BERT architecture that runs on a target hardware and meets user-defined performance requirements (accuracy, inference time)? (b) what are the trade-offs between accuracy and model size when we do optimizations (like pruning) to run them on the limited memory of embedded devices? and (c) what does pruning mean for accuracy and resource usage, including memory, inference time, and energy consumption? To answer these questions, we look at the overhead of running different BERT architectures on four different hardware (Raspberry Pi, Jetson Nano, UP 2, and UDOO). Our experiments show that some BERT models (specifically the "distilled" ones) did not reach the desired performance goals (e.g., F1 score) for various NLP tasks. Also, pruning can make the model smaller but it does not help much with energy efficiency.

Contributions. No prior work has deployed these models on embedded platforms, so our study fills the gap between simulation-based studies and real-world scenarios. Our findings can help designers choose other BERT-based architectures under given resource constraints, which saves development time and hassle. For reproducibility, our implementation and documentation are publicly available.

Our contributions in this paper are:

- Our study systematically looks at the performance of BERT-based language models on four off-the-shelf embedded platforms (Raspberry Pi, Jetson, UP 2, and UDOO) with two memory variants (2 GB and 4 GB RAMs). We analyzed the trade-offs between complexity and accuracy across several NLP tasks. (Sec. 3 -Sec. 4).

- We explore if complex NLP tasks can be deployed on embedded systems and analyze them with three metrics: (a) inference time, (b) memory usage, and (c) energy consumption. From empirical observations we developed a lookup table that system designers can use to decide model configurations for the target platform (Sec. 4).

Our key findings. When running the NLP tasks on our test platforms we observed: (a) simpler NLP tasks such as IC can get a relatively high (90%+) F1 score; (b) inference time is proportional to the size of the trained model and trimming the models loses some accuracy (e.g., 60% of reduction in model size could reduce the accuracy by 50%); (c) energy consumption on our test hardware stays about the same whether we prune the model or not; and (d) GPUs help to decrease inference time, but if there are no GPUs a faster CPU can make up for it.

We start with the problem statement and the selected datasets (Sec. 2). Section 3 describes our experiment setup and then we discuss our findings in Sec. 4.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The natural language processing (NLP) domain and the emergence of large language models are rapidly transforming how we interact with technology. With the proliferation of IoT-specific applications, the demand for voice-controlled services that perform tasks by responding to spoken commands is growing. Use cases of NLP applications, especially those that need embedded and mobile systems, include home automation, healthcare, industrial control, and automotive infotainment. To design a dialogue-based interaction system for a target device, we need models that can (a) run on the hardware and (b) meet the desired level of accuracy. Although some services such as digital assistants (e.g., Alexa, Siri, Cortana) can leverage cloud resources for processing human voices, there are applications (e.g., offline home/industrial robots, automotive infotainment, battlefield/military equipment) that may not have network connectivity and thus need to run NLP tasks on the embedded device itself. The challenge is understanding the feasibility of running a large language model on resource-limited devices.

Transformer-based architectures [1], especially BERT-based models [2], have established themselves as popular state-of-the-art baselines for many NLP tasks, including Intent Classification (IC), Sentiment Classification (SC), and Named Entity Recognition (NER). However, a well-known criticism of BERT-based architectures is that they are data-hungry and consume a lot of memory and energy, which makes deploying them in embedded systems challenging. Due to its excessive size (431 MB) and parameters (110 M), deploying a pre-trained BERT model (BERT_{Base}) in resource-constrained embedded devices is often impractical, especially at the production level with minimum accuracy/performance requirements. Lighter versions of BERT (e.g., DistilBERT [3] and TinyBERT [4]) often result in accuracy losses. The degree of degradation depends on the difficulty of the task, since those models often cannot perform well on complex NLP tasks such as emerging entity [5] or mixed emotion detection [6]. Designers therefore must make a trade-off between an accurate model and one that can run smoothly in a resource-constrained environment. Unfortunately, developers often have little idea about this trade-off and spend a lot of time on trial-and-error experiments to find an architecture that is feasible for the target hardware and meets a desired level of accuracy.

From a developer's perspective, it is still unclear what the "right" BERT-based architecture is for a given NLP task that strikes a suitable trade-off between the available resources and the minimum accuracy desired by the user. Due to the staggering size of the BERT_{Base} model, we experiment with different "distilled" BERT models (e.g., DistilBERT and TinyBERT) for IC, SC, and NER tasks. However, existing ready-to-use distilled models perform poorly on some SC and NER datasets (Sec. 4). Hence, there is a need to explore other models that better optimize the efficiency/accuracy trade-offs.

This research performs an exploratory study of BERT-based models under different resource constraints and accuracy budgets to derive empirical data about these resource/accuracy trade-offs. We aim to answer the following questions: (a) how can we determine a suitable BERT architecture that runs on a target hardware and meets user-defined performance requirements (accuracy, inference time)? (b) what are the trade-offs between accuracy and model size as we perform optimizations (such as pruning) to run models on limited embedded device memory? and (c) what are the implications of pruning on accuracy and the corresponding resource usage, including memory, inference time, and energy consumption? To answer these questions, we observe the overhead of running various BERT architectures on four different hardware platforms (viz., Raspberry Pi [9], Jetson Nano [10], UP 2 [11], and UDOO [12]). Our experiments suggest that some BERT models (specifically the "distilled" ones) failed to achieve the desired performance goals (e.g., F1 score) for various NLP tasks. Further, although pruning can reduce model size, it does not significantly help energy efficiency.

Contributions. Our study fills the gap between simulation-based studies and real-world scenarios, as no prior work has deployed these models on embedded platforms. Our findings can help designers choose alternative BERT-based architectures under given resource constraints, saving development time and hassle. To ensure reproducibility, our implementation and related documentation are publicly available [13].

We make the following contributions in this paper.

- • Our study systematically investigates the performance of BERT-based language models on four off-the-shelf embedded platforms (Raspberry Pi, Jetson, UP 2, and UDOO) with two different memory variants (2 GB and 4 GB RAMs). We analyze the trade-offs between complexity and accuracy across multiple NLP tasks. (Sec. 3 -Sec. 4).

- • We explore the feasibility of deploying complex NLP tasks on embedded systems and analyze them under three metrics: (a) inference time, (b) memory usage, and (c) energy consumption. Through empirical observations, we developed a lookup table that system designers can use to decide suitable model configurations for the target platform (Sec. 4).

Our key findings. Our observations from executing the NLP tasks on our test platforms are as follows: (a) simpler NLP tasks such as IC can achieve a relatively high (90%+) F1 score; (b) the time required for inference is proportional to the size of the trained model, and trimming models results in some accuracy loss (e.g., a 60% reduction in model size could reduce the accuracy by 50%); (c) the energy consumption on our test hardware remains relatively consistent whether we prune the model or not; and (d) while GPUs help decrease inference time, the lack of GPUs can be compensated by faster CPUs.

We start with the problem statement and the selected datasets (Sec. 2). Section 3 describes our experiment setup, and we discuss our findings in Sec. 4.

References:
